title: What already happened
goal: Talk about what happened using the past tense — and recognize its four ending patterns from the verb groups you learned in Unit 7.
bekal: past-tense endings for all four groups: *-ade, -de, -te, -dde*
the twenty most common strong verbs

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Måndagsmorgon
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in the campus cafeteria. Oskar looks tired, and Dian is curious where he disappeared to all weekend.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad gjorde du i helgen? Du svarade aldrig.
lines.id: What did you do this weekend? You never answered.
lines.literal: what did you in weekend-the? you answered never.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Förlåt! Jag åkte till Dalarna med min familj.
lines.id: Sorry! I went to Dalarna with my family.
lines.literal: sorry! I went to Dalarna with my family.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad kul! Hur länge var ni där?
lines.id: How fun! How long were you there?
lines.literal: what fun! how long were you-all there?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Vi åkte på fredag kväll och kom hem igår natt.
lines.id: We left on Friday evening and got home late last night.
lines.literal: we went on Friday evening and came home yesterday night.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Vi bodde i en röd stuga vid en sjö. Vi badade, fiskade och grillade.
lines.id: We stayed in a red cabin by a lake. We swam, fished and had barbecues.
lines.literal: we lived in a red cabin by a lake. we bathed, fished and grilled.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Ja! Vattnet var kallt, men vi bastade först. Det är tradition.
lines.id: Yes! The water was cold, but we had a sauna first. It's tradition.
lines.literal: yes! water-the was cold, but we sauna-ed first. it is tradition.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: And the food? What did you eat?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Vi grillade korv och åt jordgubbar. Min farmor bakade en kaka.
lines.id: We grilled sausages and ate strawberries. My grandma baked a cake.
lines.literal: we grilled sausage and ate strawberries. my father's-mother baked a cake.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nu blir jag hungrig. Och lite avundsjuk.
lines.id: Now I'm getting hungry. And a bit jealous.
lines.literal: now become I hungry. and little envious.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Följ med nästa gång! Vi åker igen i juni.
lines.id: Come along next time! We're going again in June.
lines.literal: follow with next time! we go again in June.

notes: **Swedish has one simple past form.** Where English splits "I ate" and "I was eating", Swedish uses *jag åt* for both — there is no "was …-ing" form to worry about. ("I have eaten" has its own form in Swedish too; that is Unit 16.) And just like the present tense, it is **one form for everyone**: *jag åt, du åt, vi åt, de åt*.

**Bodde, badade, fiskade, grillade** — all group 1 verbs take the long, easy-to-spot ending **-ade**. This is the biggest group, so if you are unsure, *-ade* is your best guess — think of it as Swedish "-ed".

**Åkte, bastade, var, åt, kom, gjorde** — here are verbs that don't follow the main pattern. *Var* (was/were), *åt* (ate), *kom* (came), *gjorde* (did), *gick* (went), *fick* (got) are the six past forms you will hear most in Swedish conversation, and all six are irregular — exactly as their English counterparts are.

**En stuga** is a small wooden house in the countryside — usually painted red with white corners (*faluröd*), a color that has become the trademark of the Swedish landscape. Many Swedish families own one, and spending the weekend at *stugan* is a national pastime.

**Bastade** comes from *att basta*, "to take a sauna". The word *bastu* itself is borrowed from Finnish, and the sauna-then-cold-water-swim routine is no joke: it is done in earnest, all year round, including through a hole cut in the ice.

**Jordgubbar** — strawberries, literally "earth old men". The season lasts only a few weeks in June and July, and Swedes wait for it like a holiday. A box of *jordgubbar* on the *midsommar* table is practically compulsory.

grammars.title: Past-tense endings by group
after: Whether group 2 takes **-de** or **-te** depends on the last sound of the stem: if it is voiced (*l, m, n, r, v, ng*), the ending is *-de*; if it is voiceless (*k, p, s, t, x*), it is *-te*. You don't need to memorize this — your mouth will pick whichever is easier to say, and your mouth will be right. English does the same thing with "-ed": compare the *d* in "called" with the *t* sound in "looked".
Group 1 (*-ade*) covers about 80% of all Swedish verbs, and every new verb joins it. If you meet an unfamiliar verb and need its past form, *-ade* is almost always right.
In fast speech, *-ade* is often clipped to *-a*: *jag prata* instead of *jag pratade*. You will hear it; don't copy it in writing.

grammars.title: The twenty most common strong verbs
after: **Gjorde** is pronounced **YOO-deh** — the *g* is silent and the *j* gives a *y* sound. It is the past of *göra*, and it opens the question that starts almost every Monday-morning conversation in Sweden: *Vad gjorde du i helgen?*
**Sa** is the short form of *sade*, and in conversation it is almost always *sa*. Formal writing uses *sade*, but even newspapers now write *sa*.

Notice how many have cousins in English: *drack-drank*, *sov-slept* (the same vowel change), *skrev-wrote*, *gav-gave*, *såg-saw*, *satt-sat*, *stod-stood*. English and Swedish inherited the same list of strong verbs from the same ancestor — so if an English verb is irregular, its Swedish cousin very often is too.

blocks.text: **I helgen** has a handy quirk: it means "last weekend" **and** "this coming weekend", depending on the verb form. *Vad gjorde du i helgen?* asks about the past; *Vad ska du göra i helgen?* asks about the future. The verb decides, not the time expression.

**För … sedan** is a two-part frame for "… ago": *för tre dagar sedan*, *för en vecka sedan*, *för länge sedan* (a long time ago). Both parts are required — English needs only "ago" at the end, but Swedish wraps the time in *för … sedan*. Drop *sedan* and the sentence means something else entirely.

blocks.title: Telling a story: four linking words
items: **först** — first · **sedan** — then · **efter det** — after that · **till slut** — finally
*Först åkte vi till Dalarna. Sedan badade vi i sjön. Efter det grillade vi korv. Till slut somnade alla vid brasan.*
Notice that all four take first place, so the verb follows right behind them and the subject gets pushed back. The rule from Unit 3 still applies, whatever tense the verb is in.

blocks.text: **Allemansrätten** — "everyman's right" — is the Swedish rule that lets anyone walk, camp for a night, and pick berries and mushrooms in any forest, including on private land, as long as they cause no damage and keep away from people's houses. It is a right protected by law and a great source of pride. There is one condition: *inte störa, inte förstöra* — don't disturb, don't destroy.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 13
items: Give the command form of ten verbs from Unit 13 without looking.
Then put all ten into the past: *kom* → *kom*, *titta* → *tittade*, *ring* → *ringde*, *köp* → *köpte*.
Finally, tell the story of your own weekend in six past-tense sentences using *först, sedan, efter det, till slut*.

exercises.prompt: Write the past form of these strong verbs.

items: What did you do last weekend?
We went to Dalarna on Friday.
We stayed in a red cabin.

answers: badade — ringde — köpte — bodde — grillade — läste
var — gjorde — åt — kom — gick — såg
Jag åkte till Dalarna. — Vi badade i sjön. — Hon köpte en bok. — De bodde i en stuga. — Han gjorde ingenting. — Vi åt jordgubbar.
Vad gjorde du i helgen? — Vi åkte till Dalarna på fredag. — Vi bodde i en röd stuga. — Vattnet var kallt. — Min farmor bakade en kaka.
